items.paragraph: Software engineers speak of technical debt: the future cost created when code is written quickly rather than well. The metaphor is apt in one respect, since like a loan a shortcut lets a team deliver something sooner in exchange for paying more later, and taking it on can be a sensible choice. But it misleads in another. A financial debt has a known balance and a schedule of payments, so a borrower can decide whether it is worth it. The cost of hasty code is rarely visible; it shows up as features that take longer than expected and failures nobody can easily trace, and it grows in ways no one has agreed to. Teams therefore tend to take on far more of it than they would if the bill arrived in writing.

items.paragraph: The idea of a keystone species, one whose removal brings an ecosystem's arch tumbling down, has been enormously useful in persuading people that a single unremarkable creature can matter far beyond its numbers. An arch has one keystone, fixed by its geometry; in living systems the importance of a species often depends on circumstances, so that a predator that holds a community together in one bay may be of little consequence in the next, or may matter only in dry years. items.paragraph: At a symphony concert, a burst of clapping after the opening movement is often answered by hissing from seasoned listeners, who regard unbroken quiet until the final chord as a sacred inheritance. items.paragraph: Term limits for legislators are usually defended as a cure for entrenched power: if no one can hold a seat for decades, the argument goes, politics will be refreshed by newcomers who are closer to ordinary citizens. Lawmakers who must leave after a few years have little time to master budgets, procedure or the details of policy, and they come to rely on those who stay: permanent staff, party organisations and lobbyists who have spent years in the building. items.paragraph: It is sometimes said that a politician who lies to the public or bargains with a ruthless faction to prevent a greater harm has simply done the right thing, and that once the calculation favours the act, no moral residue remains. This tidy view misdescribes the situation. The act may be justified, all things considered, and still involve doing something wrong: deceiving people who were owed the truth, or lending strength to people who deserved none. A leader who felt nothing after such a choice would be more worrying than one who felt the weight of it, because that weight is how a person registers that a real claim was overridden rather than dissolved. Justification answers whether one should act; it does not erase what the act cost those it wronged.

items.paragraph: Patients often sign consent forms for procedures they do not understand, and the usual explanation is that the forms are badly written. That is part of it, but the deeper difficulty lies in conversation. Doctors learn a technical vocabulary so thoroughly that words like 'benign', 'negative' or 'unremarkable' stop sounding specialised to them, even though a patient may hear a negative result as bad news. Meanwhile patients, unwilling to appear slow or to waste a busy doctor's time, nod rather than ask. Each side leaves believing that information has been exchanged. Consent obtained in this way satisfies the paperwork while missing its purpose, which is that the person agreeing should know what they are agreeing to.

items.paragraph: Many cities require every new building to provide a minimum number of parking spaces, a rule meant to stop drivers from overwhelming the surrounding streets. The intention is sensible, but the rule carries costs that are easy to overlook because they are hidden in other prices. Parking takes land and money, so the requirement raises the cost of every flat and shop that is built, whether or not its occupants own a car; residents who do not drive in effect subsidise those who do. And by guaranteeing that driving will always be convenient, the rule encourages more of it, partly creating the demand it was meant to accommodate. None of this means a city should have no parking. It means that the amount should be decided by those who build and use it, rather than fixed by a rule that assumes everyone will drive.
